presented_options.A: it is a thin wrapper around a third-party HTTP library (hyper/httparse) configured for strict mode
presented_options.B: parsing is done lazily inside each handler on a per-need basis; there is no central parser module
presented_options.C: requests are proxied to a trusted upstream server and the parsed form is ingested; the framework itself doesn't parse HTTP
presented_options.D: it is a hand-written parser module that reads bytes directly and that no other layer reaches into — routers and middleware consume typed Request / Response values only

answers.rationale: A from-scratch framework named 'nanoweb' would implement its own hand-written HTTP parser that produces typed Request/Response values consumed by upper layers; routers and middleware never touch raw bytes.

presented_options.A: it walks a trie whose node kinds are literal / parameter / wildcard; match is O(path-length) and allocates only the parameter map
presented_options.B: it compiles all registered paths into a single regex at startup and runs captures on each request
presented_options.C: it hashes the full path and looks the handler up in a HashMap<(Method, String), Handler>
presented_options.D: it does a linear scan over a Vec<(Method, String, Handler)> and falls back to a 404 on the first non-match

answers.rationale: Production-quality routers use a trie with literal/parameter/wildcard node kinds for O(path-length) matching. Linear scan (D) is too naive; regex compilation (B) is fragile; HashMap on full path (C) can't handle parameters.

presented_options.A: an OPTIONS request on a defined route returns an Allow header listing the methods registered for that path
presented_options.B: registering GET /users automatically registers POST /users with the same handler for convenience
presented_options.C: path parameters (e.g. /users/:id) are captured and made available to the handler through a typed params map
presented_options.D: a HEAD request reuses the GET handler and omits the body from the response

answers.rationale: Automatically registering POST when GET is registered would be inconsistent with standard HTTP framework design — methods are registered explicitly. The other options (OPTIONS Allow header, path params, HEAD reusing GET) are all conventional behaviors.

presented_options.A: each middleware is a closure stored in a Vec; the chain is executed by a fold over that Vec each request
presented_options.B: each middleware implements a single object-safe trait; the chain is a list of trait objects whose registration order drives outer-to-inner call order
presented_options.C: middlewares are composed via tower::Layer and tower::Service; nanoweb re-exports the tower types
presented_options.D: middlewares are chosen per request by a proc-macro that expanded at compile time to a different fn for each route

answers.rationale: A minimal framework typically uses a single object-safe trait (e.g. Middleware) with a Vec of Box<dyn Middleware> where registration order determines outer-to-inner call order. Tower (C) would be a heavy dependency for a from-scratch crate.

presented_options.A: TLS is a required dependency; the crate does not compile without rustls
presented_options.B: TLS is gated by a Cargo feature (tls) that is enabled by default; with the feature off the crate still builds and the --tls-cert flag emits a clear error
presented_options.C: TLS is a runtime decision based on the NANOWEB_TLS env var; both code paths are always compiled
presented_options.D: TLS lives in a separate sibling crate nanoweb-tls that the main crate re-exports

answers.rationale: The idiomatic Rust pattern is a Cargo feature flag (tls, enabled by default). With the feature off, the crate still compiles but the --tls-cert flag emits a runtime error explaining TLS support was not compiled in.

presented_options.A: it stops accepting new connections, lets in-flight requests complete up to a bounded graceful_timeout_s, then exits 0
presented_options.B: it hot-reloads the config without exiting; shutdown requires SIGQUIT
presented_options.C: it drains the TCP buffers but keeps the process alive so a supervisor can signal readiness again
presented_options.D: it exits immediately; in-flight connections are dropped mid-response

answers.rationale: Standard graceful shutdown: stop accepting new connections, wait up to graceful_timeout_s for in-flight requests to complete, then exit 0. This is the expected behavior for a production-ready server.

presented_options.A: it mounts a Prometheus text-exposition endpoint at a configurable path with per-method/status/route counters and a request-duration histogram
presented_options.B: it logs one structured JSON line per request; aggregation happens downstream
presented_options.C: it writes one statsd UDP packet per request to localhost:8125
presented_options.D: it emits OpenTelemetry OTLP over gRPC to a collector configured via env var

answers.rationale: A framework with observability support most naturally exposes a Prometheus text-exposition endpoint with per-method/status/route counters and a request-duration histogram, as Prometheus scraping is the dominant pattern in Rust web services.

presented_options.A: it uses the TCP connection's 4-tuple as an implicit id; no HTTP header is set
presented_options.B: it generates a fresh id per request, attaches it to the structured log context for that request, and mirrors it to the response as X-Request-Id
presented_options.C: it correlates requests only within a session cookie; there is no per-request id
presented_options.D: it passes an inbound X-Correlation-Id through unchanged and does nothing if the header is absent

answers.rationale: Standard correlation ID handling: generate a fresh UUID per request, attach to the structured log context for that request, and echo it back as X-Request-Id in the response for client-side correlation.

presented_options.A: scattered across each consuming module — wherever a value is read, the module checks CLI then TOML
presented_options.B: inside main as a long if-else chain immediately before tokio::main boots the server
presented_options.C: inside a single config module that loads TOML, applies CLI overrides, and yields one Config struct that all other modules consume
presented_options.D: inside clap's derive macros via #[arg(default_value_from_fn)] hooks that reach into the TOML at parse time

answers.rationale: Clean architecture places all config precedence logic in a single config module that loads TOML, applies CLI overrides, and yields one Config struct. This avoids scattered precedence logic and makes the config behavior testable in isolation.

presented_options.A: a compile-time HTML macro (like maud) that produces typed HTML fragments
presented_options.B: there is no template engine; handlers build HTML by hand
presented_options.C: a full Jinja2-compatible engine with filters, macros, template inheritance, and sandboxed eval
presented_options.D: a minimal mustache-style renderer with variable interpolation ({{name}}), sections ({{#list}}{{/list}}), and inverted sections ({{^absent}}{{/absent}})

answers.rationale: A minimal framework would ship a simple mustache-style renderer with variable interpolation ({{name}}), sections ({{#list}}), and inverted sections ({{^absent}}) — lightweight enough to implement from scratch without external dependencies.

presented_options.A: logger as the outermost middleware, with basic auth among the inner middlewares
presented_options.B: logger, gzip, sliding-window rate limit per API key, CORS, OAuth2 bearer guard
presented_options.C: logger, gzip, token-bucket rate limit per client IP, CORS, double-submit-cookie CSRF, basic auth
presented_options.D: logger, gzip, rate limit, CORS, CSRF, basic auth — exactly the six types registered in the default middleware chain

answers.rationale: OAuth2 bearer guard is a heavyweight auth mechanism unlikely to be in a minimal default middleware set. The realistic default set is: logger, gzip, rate limit, CORS, CSRF, basic auth — option D describes this accurately, making B (which adds OAuth2) inconsistent.

presented_options.A: a single NanowebError enum is the return type of top-level fallible entry points; submodule errors convert at their public boundary
presented_options.B: errors are conveyed by panicking on the fallible path and recovering via catch_unwind at the accept loop
presented_options.C: each submodule exposes its own error type; the server returns Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync> and callers downcast
presented_options.D: errors are stringly typed: Result<T, String> end to end

answers.rationale: Idiomatic Rust error design uses a single top-level NanowebError enum as the public API boundary; submodule errors implement From<SubError> for NanowebError and convert at their public boundary, giving callers one type to match on.

presented_options.A: exits with code 1 because at least one request was still in flight when the timeout elapsed
presented_options.B: waits up to ~30 seconds, then exits with code 0; the two long-running handlers are abandoned mid-response
presented_options.C: waits indefinitely until every in-flight request completes, then exits with code 0
presented_options.D: aborts immediately on SIGTERM, replying 503 to all in-flight connections, then exits non-zero

answers.rationale: If the default graceful_timeout_s is ~30 seconds, the process waits up to 30s, the three short requests complete, but the two 60-second handlers are abandoned at timeout expiry. The process exits 0 since this is a clean controlled shutdown.

presented_options.A: the parser imports byte-handling helpers (std::str, the `bytes` crate, or equivalent) and the crate's `error` module
presented_options.B: the parser imports HTTP shape types (Method, Header, Version) from a sibling `http::types` (or equivalent) module
presented_options.C: the parser imports the router module (e.g. trie node types or route-match results)
presented_options.D: the parser imports its own internal helper submodules (e.g. chunked-body decoder, header folding) but nothing from outside `http::`

answers.rationale: The HTTP parser module should NOT import the router module — parsing and routing are separate concerns. The parser produces typed Request values; the router consumes them. Importing trie node types or route-match results into the parser would violate layering.
